title: There’s No Link Between Crime and Unauthorized Immigration
gist: A UC Irvine-led study of a decade of crime statistics across 11,500 U.S. neighborhoods found no evidence that growth in unauthorized immigration increases crime; neighborhoods with the largest increases in undocumented population actually saw larger drops in property crime and aggravated assault.

themes.theme: Immigration and crime as a political and empirical question

insights.claim: Immigration and crime ranked among the top five issues in the 2024 U.S. presidential election according to a Pew survey, with Trump voters rating both issues as more important than Harris voters did.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Frames the political salience of immigration-crime narratives that the new empirical study directly contradicts, relevant to ongoing U.S. immigration policy debates.
insights.quote: Unsurprisingly, Trump voters rated both issues higher than Harris voters, and combining the two (with a healthy dose of demagoguery) proved to be enough to sweep Trump into the White House for a second term.
insights.locator: Immigration and crime weren't the biggest issues

insights.claim: A large-scale study published in the Journal of Urban Affairs, led by researchers at the University of California, Irvine, examined a decade of crime statistics across 11,500 U.S. neighborhoods and found no evidence that increases in unauthorized immigration drove up crime.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Provides large-sample, neighborhood-level empirical evidence directly countering a politically salient claim linking unauthorized immigration to rising crime.
insights.quote: Combing through crime statistics spanning a decade from 11,500 neighborhoods, a team led by researchers at the University of California, Irvine found no evidence that an increase in unauthorized immigration drove up crime.

insights.claim: Neighborhoods that saw the largest growth in undocumented immigrant population actually saw greater reductions in property crime and aggravated assaults, according to the UC Irvine-led study.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The direction of the effect is not just null but inverse — larger undocumented population growth correlated with bigger crime declines, a striking finding for policy debates on immigration enforcement.
insights.quote: In fact, the neighborhoods that saw the largest growth in the population of undocumented immigrants actually saw greater reductions in property crime and aggravated assaults.

insights.claim: Study author Charis E. Kubrin of UC Irvine said the finding that unauthorized immigration doesn't drive crime rates is consistent with the broader research base and was not surprising to her.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The lead researcher frames this result as consistent with prior criminology literature, not an outlier finding, strengthening its credibility as representative of the field's consensus.
insights.quote: “Consistent with the research base more generally, unauthorized immigration doesn’t drive crime rates in U.S. neighborhoods,” study author Charis E. Kubrin of UC Irvine said in a statement. “Honestly, I wasn’t too surprised.”
